source: Battambang Provincial Department of Agriculture and the Cambodia Northwest Provinces Fruit Culture Development Committee (financial support from the SEILA Programme), Khmer translation of Photpeechon Whayooathdee, "ដំណាំខ្នុរ (Jackfruit)", "Translation Copy No. 4", January 1997 (500 copies printed). This is a Khmer translation of a Thai-language original: Whayooathdee, Photpeechon, "Jackfruit (2nd edition)", Nonthaburi Province, Thailand: Agriculture Lover's Printing House, 1988. Cover illustration source: Forestry/Fuelwood Research and Development Project, 1992, "Growing Multipurpose Trees on Small Farms", Winrock International, Bangkok. Other artwork by Sarath, Som, Center for Social Development, Phnom Penh, Dec. 1996.
text:
Jackfruit is grown widely across many countries, and different communities have long applied the general term "ខ្នុរ" (khnor) loosely to a broad group of related fruits without strict agreement on which precise botanical species each name refers to. This looseness in common naming is the root of a persistent confusion: people in different regions may use the same common name for genuinely different species, or use different common names for what is botanically the same species. The book opens by explaining that without a clear, agreed classification, farmers and traders cannot reliably communicate about which variety or species they are actually discussing, which has practical consequences for selecting planting material and for trade.

According to the source, in the Buddhist Era year 2525 (1982 CE), a professional meeting of agricultural/forestry specialists (the text references a conference tied to the Royal Forest Department era) undertook to formalize and standardize the naming of jackfruit-group trees, distinguishing the true jackfruit ("ខ្នុរ") from related look-alike species and from named local varieties. The text notes this standardization effort was necessary because, prior to it, various local names were used inconsistently between regions, and it recommends that anyone discussing jackfruit varieties first clarify precisely which named type they mean.

Note on translation confidence: several of the specific local/cultivar names transliterated on these pages (rendered in the source with Khmer diacritics referring to Thai common names) are difficult to render with full certainty from the scanned text; where a name could not be read with confidence it has been omitted here rather than guessed, in line with the instruction not to invent specific names.
